content: 1. Caregivers often face challenges that prevent them from effectively using Care for Child Development (CCD) interventions. These challenges include identifying and addressing barriers that hinder their ability to stimulate their child’s development. One of the least commonly used components of the intervention is asking caregivers about the specific actions they take to stimulate their child or providing counseling on how to enhance their child’s developmental progress. Demonstrating the use of homemade toys and helping caregivers find solutions to these challenges are also less frequently utilized. 2. In your opinion, most providers who have undergone training for CCD view this intervention as a fundamental part of their practice. However, some may not consider it a core component of their professional responsibilities. 3. The primary obstacles to the effective use of CCD include insufficient training, inadequate supervision or feedback, lack of value placed on CCD by providers, limited time allocated per child visit, and other context-specific barriers. 4. To address these challenges, the project team has developed several strategies. These include appointing a designated supervisor to provide support to implementers, identifying a ‘champion’ to lead the implementation process, and organizing regular group meetings for feedback and support. 5. Over the next three years, CCD will be implemented in your country by training a specific number of providers from various professional backgrounds. These providers will counsel a targeted number of children and caregivers using CCD principles. 6. Support from organizations such as WHO and UNICEF is essential for the successful implementation of CCD in your country. This support may include additional resources, training materials, or technical guidance. 7. CCD is being implemented across various systems, including the healthcare system, education system, social services, non-governmental organizations, and academic institutions. Other systems may also be involved depending on the local context. 8. Positive changes observed in communities as a result of CCD include improved caregiver knowledge, enhanced child development outcomes, and strengthened family relationships. Specific examples of these changes should be documented to highlight the impact of the intervention. 9. Key factors contributing to these positive changes include effective training, community engagement, and the availability of resources to support caregivers in implementing CCD practices. 10. Changes in the systems where CCD is implemented may include improved integration of child development services, enhanced collaboration between sectors, and the establishment of monitoring and evaluation mechanisms. 11. In the next two years, additional positive changes are expected in both communities and systems. These may include increased caregiver participation, better developmental outcomes for children, and stronger institutional support for CCD. 12. The date of the CCD training, the methods used for training, and the inclusion of clinical practice sessions are critical details to document. Trainers’ affiliations and preparation levels should also be noted. 13. The number and professional backgrounds of providers trained in CCD should be recorded, including nurses, general physicians, pediatricians, child development specialists, psychologists, educators, social workers, and paraprofessionals. 14. Providers should indicate their age, gender, occupation, and workplace type, such as primary healthcare centers, hospitals, or social service centers. The number of children served daily and the frequency of home visits should also be documented. 15. Providers should report whether they have received any training related to child development other than CCD and describe how they currently use CCD in their practice. This includes whether they use CCD cards, provide handouts, or demonstrate toys to caregivers. 16. Barriers to using CCD with all child-caregiver clients should be identified. These may include time constraints, inadequate training, lack of user-friendly materials, or caregiver disinterest. Providers should indicate the most significant barrier they face. 17. Systems for supervision and feedback related to CCD should be in place, and providers should report how often they receive such support and from whom. 18. Factors that facilitate the use of CCD include home visits, well-child care visits, sufficient time with clients, and continuity of care with the same families over time. Providers should identify the most important factor that supports their use of CCD. 19. Providers should outline any plans to improve their use of CCD in the future and provide three specific suggestions to enhance the intervention’s effectiveness in promoting child development. 20.
